#BREAKING In what the Bench confirmed is the first ruling by any Supreme Court on the issue, the Supreme Court of India holds that a valid contractual notice is sufficient to terminate a bareboat charter. Physical repossession or redelivery of the vessel is not a precondition for termination.

The Court holds that after termination, the former charterer’s continuing possession is only as a gratuitous bailee. A maritime creditor cannot arrest the vessel for that entity’s liabilities if it was no longer the demise charterer when the arrest was effected.

The Court allows the appeal and sets aside the arrest of MV Nereus Progress, finding that its charter stood terminated on November 13, 2025, before its arrest on December 4.

When counsel said this was the first judgment by any Supreme Court on the subject, CJI Surya Kant said: “We have distinguished the Hong Kong and Singapore judgments also in our judgment. And yes, indeed.”

The Bombay High Court on Friday struck down the amendments to Information Technology (IT) Rules allowing the Central government to establish Fact-Check Units.

Different evidence produces different posterior beliefs.
Different values produce different preferences.
All of this is normal.
But before disagreement becomes productive, participants must inhabit approximately the same logical universe.
If one person says, “Here is evidence A supporting proposition B,” and the other responds, “Yes, but dolphins are mammals,” the difficulty is not ideological polarization.
It is navigation.
We need coordinates.
Your tweet gives us none.
Therefore, before I can disagree with you, I first need to locate you intellectually.
Longitude unknown.
Latitude unknown.
Altitude concerning.
Please activate semantic GPS.
There is also a possibility that your comment is satire.
If so, congratulations.
You have successfully created a text indistinguishable from sincere confusion.
This is one of satire’s greatest technical achievements.
If, however, it was sincere, then congratulations again.
You have accidentally achieved the same thing.
Either way, the artifact is remarkably stable across interpretations.
Finally, after this exhaustive multidisciplinary review, encompassing philosophy, mathematics, physics, biology, economics, history, engineering, linguistics, meteorology, gastronomy, maritime navigation, cheese, elephants, infrastructure, astronomy, architecture, jurisprudence, transportation, thermodynamics, and a hypothetical duck that has not yet been introduced but whose opinion I nevertheless respect, I am prepared to offer a provisional conclusion.
Your tweet appears to exist.
It was posted.
It contains characters.
Some characters form words.
Several words form sentences.
The sentences are arranged in an order.
Beyond that, certainty declines rapidly.
I cannot exclude the possibility that somewhere beneath the confidence, punctuation, implication, and rhetorical exhaust there is a meaningful proposition waiting to be excavated.
Perhaps future generations, equipped with better instruments, larger language models, improved archaeological techniques, and considerably more patience, will uncover it.
Until then, I recommend preserving the tweet exactly as it is.
Do not edit it.
Do not clarify it.
Do not provide evidence.
Its scientific value lies precisely in its current state.
Museums preserve fossils.
Libraries preserve manuscripts.
Natural-history collections preserve unusual specimens.
The internet should preserve this.
Future students may stand before a screenshot and ask:
“Professor, did people really argue like this?”
And the professor will look toward the window, pause for a long time, and say:
“Yes.
And sometimes they paid for a blue checkmark.”
The class will fall silent.
Outside, a bird will land on a tree.
The bird will have no opinion on the matter.
This will immediately make it one of the strongest participants in the debate.
A light breeze will move through the leaves.
Somewhere, a refrigerator will hum.
Markets will open and close.
Tides will rise and fall.
The Earth will continue rotating at approximately 1,670 km/h at the equator.
And your argument, untouched by these developments, will remain exactly where we found it:
confident,
immovable,
and still waiting for a premise.
Thank you again for your contribution.
Further research is required.

Grass H1 2026 Revenue Attestation: Looking Beyond the Headlines

Grass has released a revenue attestation covering its business activity through the first half of 2026, providing an important piece of information for anyone following the development of the Grass ecosystem, decentralized data infrastructure, and the broader intersection between crypto and AI.

At first glance, the headline numbers are simple.

Grass DataCo reported $14.53 million in revenue for the first six months of 2026.

But the more interesting part is not simply the size of that number.

The real story is how that revenue was generated, how much could already be traced to actual cash receipts, what remained outstanding, and what these figures potentially tell us about the maturity of Grass as a real-world data infrastructure business.

According to Regen Financial's report, the review covered 100% of Grass DataCo's Work Order population for both reporting periods. The first period covered March 14, 2025 through December 31, 2025, while the second period covered January 1, 2026 through June 30, 2026.

For H1 2026, Grass reported $14,527,555.66 in revenue.

Of that amount, $11,351,405.66 was substantiated through cash receipts.

The remaining $3,176,150 had not yet been substantiated by cash receipts at the time of the procedures.

That distinction is extremely important.

It means the report should not simply be interpreted as "$14.5 million in cash collected."

Instead, there is a difference between revenue recognized through signed customer Work Orders and revenue that had already been received in cash.

This is a normal distinction that can appear in businesses with contracts, invoicing cycles, and longer delivery periods.

The report specifically states that the difference was related primarily to work still in progress under long-term contracts and invoices that had been issued but not yet paid.

For H1 2026, $1.68275 million was associated with work still in progress under long-term contracts.

Another $1.4934 million represented invoiced amounts for which payment had not yet been received.

Together, these two categories account for the entire $3.17615 million difference.

This is one of the most important parts of the document because it gives additional context to the headline revenue figure.

 The bigger picture

When H1 2026 is combined with the previous reporting period, Grass DataCo reported total revenue of $32.114 million.

The breakdown is:

2025 reporting period:

$17.5869 million reported revenue

$16.2395 million substantiated by cash receipts

2026 H1:

$14.5276 million reported revenue

$11.3514 million substantiated by cash receipts

Combined:

$32.1145 million reported revenue

$27.5909 million substantiated by cash receipts

This provides a useful indication that Grass DataCo is not simply presenting a theoretical business model.

There are signed customer Work Orders, commercial relationships, invoices, contracts, and actual cash receipts behind the reported activity.

The report states that all reported revenue relates to real, signed Work Orders with customers.

That matters because one of the biggest questions surrounding decentralized infrastructure projects is whether their activity represents genuine commercial demand or primarily comes from incentives, token speculation, or ecosystem participation.

This document provides evidence of an underlying commercial business operating alongside the crypto ecosystem.

## H1 2026 is particularly interesting

The H1 2026 number deserves attention because $14.53 million of reported revenue was generated during only six months.

That means Grass DataCo's reported H1 revenue represented a substantial amount of commercial activity in a relatively short period.

However, it is important not to automatically annualize this number and assume that Grass will generate exactly twice that amount.

Revenue can be uneven.

Contracts can start and finish at different times.

Customers can have different payment schedules.

Long-term contracts can create significant timing differences between work performed, invoices issued, and cash received.

Therefore, the H1 number should primarily be viewed as evidence of commercial activity during the specific reporting period rather than a guaranteed forecast for the full year.

 Why the $11.35 million cash figure matters

The $11.35 million in cash receipts is arguably one of the most useful numbers in the document.

Cash receipts provide a more tangible connection between reported commercial activity and money actually received by the company.

The report says Regen Financial traced the Work Orders back to the underlying cash receipts and reviewed 100% of the company's Work Order population for the periods covered.

This does not mean that the report is an audit.

In fact, the document explicitly states that the engagement was a due diligence engagement rather than an audit, review, or other assurance engagement under a professional standard.

That limitation should be taken seriously.

The report does not provide an audit opinion on Grass DataCo's financial statements.

Instead, it describes procedures performed to substantiate revenue and explains the difference between reported revenue and cash receipts.

That makes the report useful for due diligence, but it should not be interpreted as equivalent to audited financial statements.

## Understanding the $3.17 million difference

The $3.17615 million difference in H1 2026 may initially look concerning if viewed without context.

But the report provides a specific explanation.

Approximately $1.683 million was related to work still in progress under long-term contracts.

Another $1.493 million was invoiced but not yet received.

This is important because revenue and cash flow do not necessarily happen at the same time.

Imagine a customer signs a large contract.

Grass begins performing the work.

The company recognizes revenue according to the relevant commercial arrangement.

But the contract may include delivery milestones and payment terms.

The cash could arrive weeks or months later.

That creates a temporary difference between reported revenue and cash receipts.

The report specifically notes that some Grass DataCo contracts can have extended delivery periods and payment terms of up to 60 days.

Therefore, the existence of a gap does not automatically mean that the underlying revenue is invalid.

At the same time, investors and observers should remember that unpaid invoices still carry collection risk.

Revenue that has been recognized but has not yet been collected is different from cash sitting in a bank account.

That distinction becomes particularly important when evaluating the financial strength of a company.

## What this says about Grass as a business

Perhaps the most interesting implication of the report is that Grass appears to have developed beyond the simple concept of a crypto-powered bandwidth network.

The broader Grass thesis has always been connected to data.

Users contribute unused internet resources.

The network aggregates that distributed capacity.

The resulting infrastructure can then support data-related applications.

The economic question is whether companies are willing to pay for access to that infrastructure.

The revenue attestation provides evidence that there are commercial Work Orders associated with Grass DataCo.

That does not prove that the entire Grass ecosystem will succeed.

But it does provide an important data point:

There is documented commercial activity behind the infrastructure.

This changes the way the project can be analyzed.

Instead of looking exclusively at token price, node participation, points, rewards, or community growth, observers can also examine the underlying business.

How much revenue is being generated?

Who are the customers?

How long are contracts?

How quickly are invoices paid?

How much revenue becomes cash?

How sustainable are margins?

How dependent is the business on a small number of customers?

These questions become increasingly important as the project matures.

## Revenue is not the same as profit

Another important distinction is that the attestation focuses on revenue.

Revenue does not tell us how profitable the company is.

A business can generate significant revenue while spending heavily on infrastructure, employee salaries, cloud services, data acquisition, sales, marketing, token incentives, and other operational expenses.

Therefore, this report should not be interpreted as proof that Grass DataCo is profitable.

To evaluate the overall financial health of the business, additional information would be required.

For example:

Operating expenses.

Gross margins.

Net income.

Cash reserves.

Accounts receivable aging.

Customer concentration.

Capital expenditures.

Token-related liabilities or expenses.

Future contractual commitments.

Without these figures, revenue provides only one part of the financial picture.

## The strategic importance of real customers

For decentralized infrastructure projects, commercial demand is arguably one of the most important long-term variables.

A network can have thousands or millions of participants.

It can have an active community.

It can have a token.

It can have impressive technical infrastructure.

But ultimately, sustainable economic activity requires demand.

The existence of signed customer Work Orders indicates that Grass DataCo has customers purchasing its services.

This is potentially significant because it connects the decentralized supply side of the Grass ecosystem with a conventional commercial demand side.

On one side:

Users contribute resources.

On the other:

Businesses purchase data-related services.

Between them:

Grass attempts to create an infrastructure layer capable of coordinating this activity.

That is the core economic experiment.

## Why the model is interesting for AI

The timing is also notable.

Artificial intelligence companies increasingly require enormous quantities of data.

Training, evaluation, search, model improvement, agent systems, and real-time applications all depend on access to information.

Traditional data infrastructure can be expensive and concentrated.

Grass is attempting to approach this problem from a decentralized infrastructure perspective.

If distributed networks can provide useful data at competitive economics, they could become another component in the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure stack.

But again, the key word is "if."

The business must demonstrate that decentralized infrastructure can provide the necessary quality, reliability, scalability, compliance, and economics required by professional customers.

Revenue provides one signal that demand exists.

It does not by itself prove that Grass has solved all of these problems.

## The difference between network growth and business growth

This is another area where Grass deserves deeper analysis.

Crypto communities often focus on network metrics.

Number of users.

Number of nodes.

Points.

Tokens distributed.

Daily activity.

Wallets.

Transactions.

These metrics can be useful.

But they do not necessarily translate into sustainable revenue.

The attestation introduces a different metric:

Commercial revenue.

That is valuable because it measures something outside the immediate crypto incentive loop.

A user running a node because they expect rewards is one type of activity.

A business signing a commercial Work Order because it needs a service is fundamentally different.

The second represents direct market demand.

Therefore, one of the most interesting metrics to follow going forward is not simply how many people participate in Grass.

It is how commercial revenue evolves relative to network growth.

If network capacity grows while commercial demand grows alongside it, that could provide evidence of stronger utilization.

If network participation increases much faster than revenue, questions about monetization and efficiency become more relevant.

This is where future disclosures could become especially informative.

## The cash conversion question

The H1 figures also create another useful metric to monitor.

Grass reported approximately $14.53 million in H1 revenue and $11.35 million in substantiated cash receipts.

That means roughly 78% of the reported H1 revenue had been substantiated by cash receipts at the time of the procedures.

The remaining portion had not yet been received or was associated with work still in progress and timing differences.

This should not be interpreted as a permanent "cash conversion rate."

It is simply the relationship between the reported revenue population and cash receipts that had been substantiated at the date of the procedures.

Timing matters.

As outstanding invoices are collected and work-in-progress contracts are invoiced, the gap could change.

For future periods, the trend will be more informative than any single percentage.

If reported revenue grows and cash receipts consistently follow, that would provide one type of signal.

If the gap continually expands, observers would naturally want to understand why.

## What the report does not tell us

There are several important questions that remain unanswered by this document.

First, the report does not provide a detailed breakdown of customers.

We do not see a complete customer concentration analysis.

Second, it does not provide profit margins.

Third, it does not provide a full balance sheet.

Fourth, it does not establish the long-term economics of the Grass token.

Fifth, it does not guarantee future revenue.

Sixth, it does not constitute an audit.

Seventh, it does not independently establish the future valuation of the Grass ecosystem.

These limitations are important because crypto markets can quickly transform a positive business-development announcement into expectations that go far beyond what the underlying document actually says.

The document should be read for what it demonstrates, not what people might want it to demonstrate.

## The bigger Grass thesis

The most interesting way to view Grass may be as an attempt to connect three different worlds.

The first is decentralized physical and digital infrastructure.

The second is data.

The third is artificial intelligence.

Users provide distributed resources.

Grass coordinates that infrastructure.

Data becomes the economic output.

Businesses and AI-related applications create demand.

The resulting commercial revenue potentially creates an economic foundation for the ecosystem.

If that model scales, Grass becomes more than a token or a decentralized bandwidth network.

It becomes a marketplace for distributed data infrastructure.

That is a much larger thesis.

But it also creates much larger requirements.

Reliability becomes important.

Data quality becomes important.

Customer retention becomes important.

Compliance becomes important.

Unit economics become important.

And eventually, profitability becomes important.

## The key takeaway

The H1 2026 attestation should not be reduced to a single headline saying "$14.5 million revenue."

The more meaningful story is the structure behind that number.

Grass DataCo reported $14.53 million in revenue during the first half of 2026.

Regen Financial reported that $11.35 million was substantiated through cash receipts.

The remaining $3.18 million was primarily associated with long-term work still in progress and invoices that had not yet been paid.

Across the entire reviewed period, Grass DataCo reported $32.11 million of revenue, with $27.59 million substantiated by cash receipts.

The report also states that 100% of the Work Order population for the covered periods was reviewed.

At the same time, Regen Financial explicitly describes the engagement as due diligence rather than an audit or assurance engagement.

That distinction should remain at the center of any serious analysis.

For Grass, the next stage is no longer simply demonstrating that the network can attract users.

The bigger challenge is demonstrating that the network can continuously convert infrastructure into valuable data services, convert those services into recurring commercial demand, and convert that demand into sustainable cash flow.

That is ultimately the metric that matters.

The H1 2026 attestation provides an important piece of evidence that a real commercial business exists underneath the Grass ecosystem. @grass #grass 

The next chapters will be about scale, customer retention, revenue quality, cash collection, margins, and the ability to turn decentralized infrastructure into a durable business.

And that is where the Grass story becomes much more interesting than a simple crypto narrative.

ఎప్పుడో 1922లో బ్రిటీష్ వాళ్లు తీసుకొచ్చిన కాలంచెల్లిన చట్టం వాడి ఇప్పుడు బీఆర్ఎస్ నాయకుడు మన్నె క్రిశాంక్ మీద కేసు పెట్టిన విషయం వెలుగులోకి వచ్చింది.

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

text: Govt sources on why satluj was pulled off the OTT platform - Section 69A of the Indian Information Technology Act, 2000 empowers the Central Government to direct intermediaries (such as ISPs, search engines, and social media platforms) to block public access to any online information or digital content.Key Aspects of Section 69AGrounds for Blocking: Content can only be blocked if deemed necessary in the interest of:Sovereignty and integrity of IndiaDefense of IndiaSecurity of the StateFriendly relations with foreign StatesPublic orderPreventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offense related to the aboveProcedure: The directive must be based on Information Technology Rules, 2009, which outline the procedural safeguards, including recording reasons in writing and forwarding orders to a designated officer.Penalties for Non-Compliance: If an intermediary fails to comply with a blocking direction, they can face imprisonment for up to 7 years and a fine.Judicial Standing: The constitutional validity of Section 69A was challenged in the landmark Supreme Court case Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India (2015). The court upheld its constitutionality, noting that it contains adequate procedural safeguards compared to the struck-down Section 66A.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

IFF has previously explained how users whose constitutional rights are being infringed upon by the State can seek restoration of their blocked content. If you are an Indian social media user or journalist whose content has been blocked due to a government order, please write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

Breaking :

EU Council wants to abolish correspondence secrecy

The EU member states want to abolish the modern secrecy of letters. In  the EU Council, the police should be able to prosecute private chat  flows and monitor such a letter communication. Experts warn that Signal  and WhatsApp could leave the EU.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

text:
Tony assured me Marcus was good, so I agreed. Ethan settled into the chair and immediately began talking about soccer, school, and a classmate who had eaten a crayon on a dare.

For about fifteen minutes, everything seemed normal. Then Marcus moved the clippers behind Ethan’s left ear and suddenly stopped.

At almost the same moment, Ethan stopped talking.

That caught my attention.

Marcus moved a little hair aside and stared at something near Ethan’s ear for several seconds. When he looked at me through the mirror, the easy smile he had worn throughout the haircut was gone.

“What is it?”

Marcus gave the smallest shake of his head and finished the haircut without explaining. The jokes disappeared, his movements became faster, and by the time Ethan jumped from the chair, I could feel something tightening in my chest.

Outside, Ethan ran toward the candy machine.

Marcus quietly brushed loose hair from the chair.

“Check behind his left ear.”

I frowned.

“For what?”

A customer had just entered the shop, and Marcus lowered his voice.

“When you get home. Somewhere private. Look carefully.”

He refused to say anything more.

Ten minutes later, Ethan and I were standing in our kitchen. He was still excited about getting two gumballs instead of one, while I tried to act as though nothing was wrong.

“Hold still for a second.”

Ethan immediately looked worried.

“Did he mess up my haircut?”

“No. I just want to check something.”

At first, I saw nothing unusual. Then I noticed a small flesh-colored patch tucked carefully into the crease behind his left ear, positioned so perfectly that I might never have noticed it without Marcus’s warning.

Something hard was hidden underneath.

I carefully lifted one edge and found a tiny black disc pressed against Ethan’s skin. It was smooth, hard, and barely larger than a grain of rice.

I had no idea what it was.

But I knew it did not belong on my child.

“Ethan, who put this here?”

His entire expression changed. The energetic boy who had been talking nonstop only minutes earlier suddenly stared at the floor.

“I don’t know.”

“Ethan, look at me.”

He still refused.

“Who put it there?”

His voice became almost a whisper.

“Maybe the man from school.”

My stomach dropped.

“What man?”

Ethan hesitated.

“The one who knew Dad.”

Ryan, Ethan’s father, had been dead for three years.

During the previous month, Ethan had been asking more questions about him than usual. He wanted stories, photographs, and especially a visit to the storage unit where I kept Ryan’s belongings, which I had assumed was simply a grieving child trying to hold onto memories that were fading.

Now I was no longer so sure.

I called the police.

The dispatcher told me not to remove the object, to lock the doors, keep Ethan beside me, and stay away from the windows until officers arrived. About twenty minutes later, two police cars pulled up outside our house.

Officer Patel examined the object without touching it and gently began asking Ethan about the man. Slowly, he admitted the stranger had approached him several times near school and had shown him an old photograph of himself standing beside Ryan.

Then Patel asked whether the man had ever given him anything.

Ethan hesitated. Finally, he pointed toward the front hallway.

“I hid it.”

A few minutes later, officers found a black case concealed behind winter boots near the coat closet.

And suddenly, whatever was happening was much bigger than the tiny object behind my son’s ear.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.
